catalog_quote: Stress is mostly word-final, but some prefixes and suffixes shift stress away from final position, for instance, “Set₁” person endings (see Table 1) in the present (xunāˊne, xunéme “I, we read,” vāíe, vāúe ~ voúe, vāíme “you, he, we say,” enénde “they put”); the participial element of the imperfect (ašnofté-žun-e “they were hearing,” xunté-m-e “I would read,” larzāˊ-yy-e “he was trembling,” i-ništé-yy-e “he would sit”); the bé- or preverb of the subjunctive (bü´-lül-ü “let it move,” ígiru “let him get”); the negative (náfa:māne “I don’t understand,” náunue “it doesn’t cut”). Preverbs seem to attract stress: mālúe “he rubs” vs. vár-mālue “he flees,” girāˊne “I grab” vs. vé-girāne “I pick up.” Note contrasts in kué “dog,” kúe “it falls,” bózā “the goat (d.o.),” bozāˊ “the goats,” bárāž “its door,” barāˊž “for him,” dózzāmun “our thief,” dozzāˊmun “our thieves,” dozzāmún “to steal.”

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is on the final syllable of the word (nouns, plural -ā́, infinitive -mún, past participle -é all end-stressed). In finite verbs stress is morphologically placed off the final syllable: it sits on the syllable before the durative -e (i.e. on the person ending in the present, on the participial element -é- in the imperfect), and is attracted leftward onto bé-/preverbs in the subjunctive/imperative/preterit and onto negative ná-; pronominal enclitics, the object/definite marker and indefinite -ì are unstressed, yielding surface minimal pairs such as kué 'dog' vs kúe 'it falls'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any of the three sketches.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbal categories: Set1 person endings (present), imperfect participial element, bé-/preverbs of subjunctive-imperative-preterit-perfect, negative ná- take the stress; preverbs attract stress (mālúe vs vár-mālue); unstressed indefinite -ì and pronominal/object enclitics (bózā 'the goat (obj.)' vs bozā́ 'the goats'; dózzāmun 'our thief' vs dozzā́mun 'our thieves'). Sister-dialect note (Judeo-Isfahani, Stilo EIr XIV/1): stressed syllables carry low pitch and unstressed high pitch, so earlier transcriptions (Abrahamian 1936) may show stress on the wrong syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation/inflected word forms including enclitics; nominal vs verbal words behave differently (nominals final, verbs morphologically assigned). No phrase-level discussion for Gazi; the Judeo-Isfahani entry adds a sentence-intonation comparison with Tehrani/Isfahani Persian and calls for instrumental study of the Isfahan-Yazd stress-pitch system.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Gazi proper, the dialect of the town of Gaz in Borkhar district north of Isfahan (Glottolog dialect gazi1245), which is the eponymous dialect of the Glottolog language 'Gazic' gazi1243. Stilo's sketch is compiled from Eilers & Schapka's 1979 Gaz corpus, Yarshater's 1969 Gaz field notes and Zhukovskii 1888, not from Stilo's own Gazi fieldwork. Two sister dialects under the same glottocode have independently authored, fieldwork-based statements that agree (saved in the same folder): Judeo-Isfahani (jude1276; Stilo, EIr XIV/1:77-84, own fieldwork: 'Stress in Esfahani Jewish is mostly word-final..' plus the remark that stressed syllables carry LOW pitch and unstressed HIGH pitch, which misled earlier transcribers such as Abrahamian 1936) and Kuhpa'i (kuhp1234; Borjian, EIr online 'KUHPAYA ii', own fieldwork: 'generally word-final in the nominals; in verbs absorbed by negative, modal prefixes, preverbs, participial element').

sources.note: Kuhpa'i (kuhp1234), Borjian's own fieldwork: 'Stress patterns are similar to other Central Dialects, that is, generally word-final in the nominals. In verbs, the stress is absorbed by the syllable carrying the negative morpheme, modal prefixes, preverbs, and participial element, as demonstrated in Table 3. Note also the contrasts in čerā́ "light" ≠ čérā "why," yané "mortar" ≠ yáne "put!" giftemón "to take" ≠ gíftemon "we used to take."' Past-participle suffix -é stressed.
